title: Legacy system: your questions answered

content.content: Up to 100 Local Planning Authorities (LPAs) are currently preparing for submission under the legacy system (2012 regulations) by the final deadline of 31 December. This closing stage can still throw up plenty of questions, for example: Will the new National Planning and Policy Framework (NPPF) affect your examination? Do you need legal representation at hearings? And what does a firm 31 December deadline actually mean in practice? Our Professional Lead for Plans Examination, Simon Berkeley, addresses these and other popular legacy system topics.
Common questions about legacy system plans

In the summer I sat down with colleagues for a webinar about legacy system local plans. As the December 31st deadline approaches, I wanted to share some of the queries that came up in that session, and a few that have arisen since.
1. The 31 December 2026 deadline

Unsurprisingly, one of the first questions we tackled in our webinar was about the practical consequences of not hitting the submission deadline. A straightforward question on the surface - but many of you will have noted that technically the regulations do allow some flexibility, in that they allow the Secretary of State to make a direction to apply a new deadline date. If your authority is at all worried about hitting that deadline, my advice is to complete your pre-examination checklist and share it with us as early as you can. You should also contact the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) with any concerns relating to the deadline and your checklist response may assist you to articulate these.

Having said that, I want to be clear about how that provision should be treated in practice. Exercising the Secretary of State's discretion is likely to be very much the exception rather than the rule. So please, do not plan for a submission that's just a little bit after the 31st of December. Every authority should be treating this as a firm deadline. It's also worth noting that the Planning Inspectorate itself has no discretion to accept late submissions.
2. What makes a submission valid?

On the legal requirements for a valid submission, the position is set out clearly in legislation. The Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004, along with the 2012 local plan regulations, specify precisely what needs to be submitted:  you must submit your plan, you must submit your sustainability appraisal, and other specified items besides. The legacy system is winding down but there is no change in the quality of plan required or the way that the tests of soundness are applied.  Beyond the legal minimum, though, there are two things I'd really encourage you to think about. Again, I’ll stress the importance of the pre-examination checklist. Second, and just as important, is having your programme officer in place prior to the start of your examination.
3. NPPF changes won't affect your legacy examinations

Many of the questioners back in early summer were asking about the expected update to the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) and that new version has now landed. I can offer some reassurance here. It's clear that the new NPPF will apply only to plans in the new system. Plans in the legacy system will continue to be examined against earlier versions of the NPPF, and related national policy (such as the Planning Policy for Traveller Sites).
4. Proportionate evidence: clarity over volume

When we're asked what a ‘proportionate evidence’ base actually looks like, I always come back to the same underlying principle: proportionality is all about the scope, depth and currency of evidence being proportionate to the local context, and the extent to which the issue in hand affects bringing forward the development that's needed. Crucially, clarity often matters more than sheer volume. Sometimes proportionate looks like things being clearly explained, concisely. That can often be more important, frankly, than volume, particularly where the evidence in question is relying on planning judgements. Do be very clear about that. Our  Procedure Guide (legacy system) provides some good general advice on the proportionality and currency of the evidence base.
5. Viability evidence: transparency over certainty

On viability evidence involving future or uncertain funding, my advice centres on transparency. Your assumptions really need to be set out transparently, and really clearly articulated, so that the inspector can be in absolutely no doubt as to what assumptions have been made, and how critical those assumptions are.  We do recognise the real-world limits of certainty around viability and around sources of future funding, and we absolutely recognise that. But at the same time, we also expect realism, and it's right that we do.  The Planning Practice Guidance on viability remains an important element of how these matters are tested at an examination along with the recent letter to us on this topic from the Minister.
6. Cross-boundary engagement still matters, even without the duty to cooperate

With the duty to cooperate now removed, a lot of authorities have asked what evidence of cross-boundary working is still necessary. My answer is that the need for engagement itself hasn't gone away. It's still very, very important. The government's been clear that yes, the duty has gone, but you should still continue engaging with your neighbours, with statutory consultees, and so on.

In evidential terms, little has really changed. You're still going to need to demonstrate what engagement you've done, with whom, and when, and what the outcomes were. Statements of common ground and memorandums of understanding also remain important.
7. Gypsy and Traveller site provision

The question was posed in the webinar: what is the advice where no deliverable Gypsy and Traveller sites are coming forward? We'll first look at whether the site search has been exhaustive. The Inspector is going to want to make sure that, in effect, the authority has done all that it reasonably could to identify sites in the first instance.

If not, the next step is neighbouring authorities. What has the authority done in terms of engaging with neighbouring authorities, and asking them whether they might be able to help meet that need? Evidence of engagement with landowners is also expected. A policy-based approach, rather than allocating specific sites, is possible, but it's harder to justify at scale. That approach needs to be justified, and it can be, perhaps, where the identified need is relatively very small, but it's unlikely to be found justified where you've got a much larger scale of need to meet.  If a policy-based approach is included in your plan, an Inspector is likely to look at the Council’s track record of delivering sites through the planning system on the basis of any similar policies in previously adopted plans for the area.  This may help with a consideration of the overall effectiveness of such an approach.
It's also worth remembering that the Public Sector Equality Duty becomes engaged in relation to this issue as well – both for the Council and the Inspector.
8. Legal representation at hearings: helpful, not required

On legal representation, I want to be clear: it is absolutely not a requirement. No authority, or any participant for that matter, needs or must have legal representation at hearings. That said, in my experience, advocates can add real value. They have particular skills in marshalling evidence and bringing it forward in a very logical way that's easy for the Inspector to follow.   The hearings remain inquisitorial Inspector-led discussions rather than adversarial, so preparation counts for more than representation. We're focused on the evidence and the clarity of the arguments put, not on the qualifications or stye of the presenter. Good preparation can be more important than representation in that respect.
9. Updating evidence mid-examination: leave it to your Inspector

On whether to refresh ‘dated’ evidence during a lengthy examination, my advice is once you have submitted to let the process run its course. The Inspector will direct the authority on this, so authorities don’t need to be worrying about this unprompted. Given how close we are to the legacy deadline, Inspectors are likely to look for alternatives to requiring fresh evidence. We're far more likely to look at what alternative approaches we might be able to take, such as whether this plan needs to be updated early, even perhaps as soon as it's adopted if that would appear to be an effective and reasonable option. My key message here is: if you're at examination, leave it to your Inspector.
We also covered housing need and requirement, site selection and spatial strategy and housing land supply and trajectories. Watch the full webinar here.

title: Plan, Prepare, Progress: reflections from our new system local plan  webinar

content.content: The transition to the new local plan system is the most significant change to plan-making in a generation. Following our Plan, Prepare, Progress webinar in July and the subsequent publication of the new National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF), Simon Berkeley, Professional Lead for Plans Examination, has taken a closer look at the questions raised by local planning authorities, and what they tell us about the road ahead.

Back in July, we had over 700 attendees at our Plan, Prepare, Progress webinar, with a lot of questions raised during the session. We've now had a chance to go back through those questions in detail, and I wanted to use this blog to share some of the strongest themes that emerged, along with our responses. We're conscious that many of you are grappling with similar issues at the same time, so if you were not able to join us live, or if your question did not get answered on the day, we hope this gives you the wider picture.
Timetables, and what happens if things slip

Understandably, the 30-month timescale was one of the biggest topics of the session. We know that many of the pressures on that timetable, particularly delays in externally produced evidence, sit largely outside a Local Planning Authority’s (LPA) direct control. Several LPAs shared real examples of the high demand and longer lead times currently for third party consultancy and receipt of material from other statutory consultees. We don't underestimate the challenges this brings, and we have heard your concerns.

I'd like to emphasise that the 30-month timeframe is a clear government expectation, rather than a statutory deadline with automatic penalties attached. The mechanism for managing any third party induced slippage is the local plan timetable itself: keeping it realistic, keeping it updated, and telling us as early as possible when things change. Early notice means we at the Planning Inspectorate can plan our resourcing properly, allocating assessor and Inspector time appropriately whereas late notification risks compounding delays further down the line.My colleagues from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) noted in the webinar that ministerial intervention remains a power in reserve for the most severe cases, but it's very much a last resort rather than a default response, and the department’s current focus is firmly on supporting authorities rather than intervention.
Gateway 2: an opportunity, not a hurdle

Several of you asked what happens if you ‘fail’ Gateway 2, and whether the clock stops while you get things ready to try again. I’m glad this was raised so that we can clear up any misunderstanding: Gateway 2 isn't a 'pass or fail' stage. It's designed to give you an Inspector's observations and advice to help you progress towards consultation, Gateway 3, and submission. We'd encourage LPAs to think of it as a genuine opportunity for support and feedback, not a ‘hurdle’ to be cleared.

The more you're able to share at Gateway 2, including draft policies, policy options, or emerging thinking on spatial strategy, even where it's not yet been through member sign-off, the more useful the feedback we can offer. We recognise the governance sensitivities this raises, particularly around publishing draft material that could shift before it is finalised to be presented for consultation. There are practical ways to manage this: use your own redaction policies where things may be commercially sensitive, label figures or wording as provisional or pre-decision where appropriate and be clear in your covering letters about what's still subject to sign-off. Draft plans and policies maps remain optional at Gateway 2, so LPAs are also free to provide narrative detail on emerging thinking rather than a fully mapped, working document if that feels more appropriate.
Local government reorganisation

Many questions reflected the genuine complexity that local government reorganisation is creating for plan-making, particularly around shifting geographies, timing, and how joint working arrangements should adapt. This came through as one of the most frequently raised issues of the day - something that was no surprise to colleagues in MHCLG who are aware of and responding to the demands on local government at this time.Of course, since this webinar was broadcast in early July there have been significant announcements regarding Local Government Reorganisation (LGR). Further guidance for LPAs affected by Local Government Reorganisation is available here pointing towards MHCLG's commitment to bringing forward transitional arrangements to help support plan-making during the transition. In the meantime, the message to LPAs is that plan-making should continue in line with the timing set out in the 2026 Regulations. If your authority is facing significant challenges as a result of these LGR changes, my colleagues at MHCLG ask that you contact them at the earliest opportunity. Evidence production came up frequently in our webinar, from playing pitch assessments to strategic flood risk work, and understandably so. Many of you are already procuring and producing evidence to meet current timescales and asked whether this work might need to be redone later to fit new standards. We want to reassure you that the intention behind data standards and digital approaches is to improve consistency and reduce duplication, not to require authorities to recreate evidence they've already properly prepared.
Evidence, resourcing and getting ahead of the curve

As an Inspector with decades of field work experience, I’m reassured that our joint advice remains much the same as it has always been – identify what evidence you'll need as early as possible and start planning for it now, rather than waiting until a gateway is imminent. Some things never change! We recognise that much of this depends on third parties, including consultants and statutory bodies, whose capacity sits outside our direct oversight. MHCLG, along with the Planning Inspectorate continue to work on guidance, data standards and the model plan to support a more proportionate and consistent approach to evidence over time.
Digital services and accessibility

Several questions touched on the balance between digitisation and accessibility. We don’t believe these should be viewed as competing pressures but rather ‘parallel obligations’. Not every stakeholder has the same level of digital capability, and LPAs will need to continue following their accessibility policies throughout the local planning process. The digital services being developed, including the Planning Inspectorate’s new examination portal currently in development (introduced in the webinar and in this blog) , are intended to complement what LPAs already publish on their examination websites.
Where to find more, and what's next

If you'd like to go back through the guidance we discussed, the best place to start is the Create or Update a Local Plan website, alongside the New Local Plan-making System Roadmap, which sets out the sequencing of guidance still to come. Both are being updated regularly, so it's worth checking back or signing up for alerts. We have also recently published our first edition of the Procedure Guide for new system plans. Again, this is likely to evolve further as the system beds in, and our digital examination service is more fully developed.

We'll continue to share updates and insights on the new system, and your feedback will help inform future content. If there are topics you'd find particularly useful for us to explore, we'd be pleased to hear your suggestions. We know the next 18 months or so are asking a great deal of local planning authorities whether you are working at pace towards the 31 December submission deadline in the legacy system or embarking on your planning journey in the new system. We don't take that for granted, and we're genuinely trying to build a system, and a working relationship with you, that reflects what we’re hearing from you.

title: Local plans: we want your feedback on the new plans service

content.content: A new digital service (GOV.UK) for Local Planning Authorities (LPAs) called Submit Development Plans is under construction now and will be available for the first new system local plans as they reach Gateway 2 in early 2027. Ben Duckworth, Digital Lead for this service, outlines what to expect from our first digital service for plans and your chance to tell the team developing it what works best for you.

As the way that plans move through examination is changing, at the Planning Inspectorate we are building a service to make the submission and management of the new local plan simpler and faster. In 2027 our new portal will go live replacing what has traditionally been a very ‘manual’ system of emails and spreadsheets with clearer, more visible tracking at each stage. LPAs will be able to check their local plan’s progress at any time and maintain an online record of every stage of their examination. The service will be secure and LPAs can give access to a range of account holders – making collaboration and oversight easier.

This matters now because early 2027 isn't far off. The first cohort of authorities working through the new system will reach Gateway 2 within months, making this an important window for engagement while the service is still being shaped. Ben - who presented on the new system in the Plan, Prepare and Progress new local plan system webinar, has said the development process involves ongoing testing with LPAs and inspectors, and that examination websites - which authorities already know well - will remain part of the picture.
We want your feedback

If your authority will reach Gateway 2 in the new system next year and you have not already signed up to take part in our user testing, then we would love to speak to you. Find out more about user testing here: Volunteer to participate in research for Digital Planning with MHCLG and PINS – Fill in form

title: A quick look at...programme officers

content.content: Every local plan examination needs a programme officer (PO) to keep things moving along smoothly. With so many legacy local plans progressing towards examination, if you are aiming for a legacy submission and haven’t yet lined up your PO then now's a good time. And, as from 2027 the first POs will start taking on plans in the new system, this really is a topic for everyone involved in local plans. Here we look at what the role involves, when to appoint and the training available from the Planning Inspectorate.
What is a programme officer ?

The Programme Officer is the person who keeps everything connected and moving in a local plan examination, they could be described as part administrative support and part project manager. They sit at the centre of communications between the inspector, the local planning authority and other participants throughout the process and the role operates with a degree of autonomy and responsibility.
Why are we talking about this now?

With a record number of local plan examinations expected over the next 12 months, experienced POs are going to be in high demand. Deciding your approach early, ideally well before submission, puts you in a much stronger position, with time to consider options and take up training.
What does the PO do?

The PO handles all the administration that keeps an examination running - managing correspondence between the Inspector and participants, coordinating hearings, maintaining the examination website and document library, and handling the representor database. Outside hearing sessions, all contact with the Inspector flows through them.
When's  the right time to appoint?

The earlier the better. Ideally by Regulation 19 stage, so they can get across the representations and help set up the examination website and document library from the start. Independent POs may book jobs well in advance. The Planning Inspectorate will ask for your PO's contact details before appointing an inspector.
Who can we appoint?

There are two main options – external or in-house. To source external programme officers, LPAs can draw on the experienced independent POs operating in the sector. A list of POs who have attended Planning Inspectorate training is available on request by emailing plans.admin@planninginspectorate.gov.uk. It's also worth knowing that an in-house appointment is a perfectly viable option - and as the free Planning Inspectorate training is available for both new and experienced POs, if you have someone suitable in mind, there's support available to bring them up to speed. The key condition for an internal appointee is that they must be separate from your planning team and have had no involvement in preparing the plan. It’s a role which requires strong project management skills and good communication and people skills.
How much of their time should we expect to need?

It varies quite a bit across the examination lifecycle and can be dependent upon the complexity of the plan being examined.  As a guide, roughly one day a week at Regulation 19 stage is typical, rising to two or three days around submission, and full-time in the run-up to and during hearings. It is important that programme officers have sufficient availability to support the examination through to its anticipated conclusion, helping to avoid delays to the process. It's worth factoring this into your budget planning early - and the PO should stay in post until the Inspector's final report is delivered.
Where can we find out more?

The full programme officer advice and the Procedure Guide for Local Plan Examinations are available on GOV.UK. Additionally, this blog gives more insights into the role. Your plans administrative team are here to provide advice - contact them at plans.admin@planninginspectorate.gov.uk.
Still weighing up your options, or want to hear it from someone who's done the job?

Earlier in the year, the Planning Advisory Service’s (PAS) Anna Rose hosted an online conversation with an independent programme officer about what the role really involves day to day, and what LPAs should be thinking about now if they haven't yet secured one.  Watch the conversation

title: How smarter banking earned Trinity Multi- Academy Trust £258,000 to put back into their school
authors: David Sheard, Group Chief Financial Officer at Trinity Multi-Academy Trust

content.content: David Sheard, Group Chief Financial Officer at Trinity Multi-Academy Trust (MAT), shares how the Department for Education (DfE) approved Insignis savings platform generated over a quarter of a million pounds in just over a year – money that is now being invested directly in opportunities for children and young people.
Our story
Trinity Multi-Academy Trust began with a single school. Today, we serve communities across 11 schools in Bradford, Calderdale, Leeds, Wakefield and Barnsley.

When people hear we generated an extra £258,000 in just over a year, they often assume we've made cuts somewhere. The reality is the opposite. By managing our cash more effectively, we've been able to invest even more in pupils - funding cooking lessons for our primary students, supporting sixth form travel and creating opportunities that otherwise wouldn't have been possible.

Like every trust, we're responsible for making every pound count. That means not only spending money wisely, but ensuring the money we hold works as hard as possible while remaining secure and fully compliant with Department for Education guidance.
By taking a more strategic approach to managing our cash balances, we generated more than £258,000 in additional income in just over 12 months.
The real story, however, isn't the money itself. It's what that money makes possible.
The numbers speak for themselves
In just over a year, we earned over £258,000 using the Insignis savings platform. That's after fees. We're projecting £350,000 for the next financial year.
But the number isn't the point.

This is money that would have sat idle in a bank account or gained low interest rates with current banking arrangements. Now it's capable of changing young people's lives. All of it funded from our central budget. It’s possible because we chose to make our money work harder.
Watch our video to hear how we used some of the income generated.
Where we started

We had up to 11 academy bank accounts across the trust. That’s one for each academy, a separate one for a private finance arrangement, plus additional accounts for our nursery and out-of-school provision.

It was complicated, time-consuming and inefficient. We were doing bank reconciliations over 11 times. We kept our reserves but earned very low interest. We weren't doing anything wrong. We just weren't doing enough.

I first heard about Insignis at a sector seminar. A fellow chief financial officer (CFO) I knew had already been using it, so I went straight to her for an honest view rather than a sales pitch. What she told me sounded good. I did my own checks, gathered references independently, and took it through our board approval process.
Insignis is the DfE approved savings platform available through the Get Help Buying for Schools service. That approval gave us a solid foundation to build our case on.
Getting started

Anyone responsible for public money is going to feel cautious. So, we started small, putting in an amount within government-protected limits. We got the money back. We got the interest. That was enough to build confidence.

Getting set up was straightforward. Insignis helped us gather references and supported us in writing a new investment policy for our trust board. The policy set out clearly what level of risk we were comfortable with. Once the board approved it, we had the green light to get started.
Within two to three months, we were using the portal actively and seeing real returns.
Choosing where to save

Some banks on savings platforms are less well known, and some have parent companies based overseas. I understand why that can feel uncomfortable when you're responsible for public funds. I felt the same way.

Insignis provides a full risk profile for every bank on the platform. Each option is graded clearly, so you can be as selective as you want. You might earn slightly less by ruling some out, but you will still earn significantly more than before.
My advice: get the risk profile, review it carefully, and let your investment policy guide your decisions.
A word on fees
Fees were one of the first concerns I raised internally. Here's my honest take.
Once you make that first transaction and see the fees come off your interest rather than your budget, you stop seeing them as a cost. You see them as a small reduction in your return.

The standard rate on the platform is around 0.2%, and it can drop to 0.1% depending on how much you deposit. Given we've earned over £258,000 after fees in just over a year, the numbers do the talking.
My message to you
I genuinely don't know why I didn't do it sooner.
There's no magic formula. Just try it. Start with a small amount you're comfortable with. Get the interest back. Watch it land in your account. That moment will change how you think about everything.

I've spoken to colleagues who say they haven't got time. I get it. We're all busy. But think of it this way: if someone guaranteed you an extra £100,000 a year, you'd find the time. And once you start, the returns make it worth every minute.
We're not here to make money. We're here to make money go further, back into our pupils and our schools. This just makes that easier to do.
Learn more about savings options for schools to see if your school or trust's money could be working harder for your pupils.

Any savings, benefits and outcomes described in this blog were provided by Trinity Multi-Academy Trust and reflect its specific experience and circumstances. Individual results will vary between schools and trusts.

title: What is Grow?
authors: Ashish Rumani, Strategy and Delivery Lead, Test, Learn and Grow

content.content: The Test, Learn and Grow programme is working to design and improve public services so that everyone, whether you use, deliver, or design them, can see and feel the difference. We believe that a more iterative, person-centred and place-based approach is the best way to get us there and we want to make it easier to work this way.
We’re trying to achieve three main things:

You've already heard about our accelerators and how we test and learn on the ground, which is the main way we are doing the first part. The ‘Grow’ part of TLG focuses on the second two: building a movement, developing capability across all layers of government and strengthening the underlying foundations that make this way of working possible. While our accelerators show what works, ‘Grow’ wants to change the system to make it easier to test and learn wherever you are.

This matters beyond our own programme. The government's wider ambition to devolve power and funding depends on national, regional and local government being able to adopt new ways of working, including new technology, quickly and confidently. Grow is one part of making those ambitions real on the ground, working with partners across all tiers of government to rewire the state and build the skills, systems and confidence needed to adopt new ways of working.
Building a Movement

We believe that, in order to have a meaningful and long-term impact, we have to build a movement around test and learn as a practice. This is so that people know about it, get excited about it and learn how to do it in their local context. We do this by working in the open (like these blogs) and sharing what we learn as we go.

We are also constantly learning from people using innovative approaches to improve public services. We know many people are doing incredible test-and-learn-style work without necessarily using that name or being part of our programme, and we want to help share their work too.
Here’s a flavour of what this looks like in practice:
You can read more about this work soon.
Increasing capability

Once people know about test and learn, they need the skills, leadership and mindsets to pursue it, wherever it happens. We are working on this across central, regional and local government, alongside the wider public, private and third sectors, all of which have important and different roles to play.

So far we’ve pushed on this by launching the Regional Capability Fund, a £10 million fund to support up to 20 places, and partner with people across different central government departments that see things the same way that we do. We’re keen to keep sharing what we learn about what works well at different levels of public service delivery, and to keep learning from others too.
Shifting the foundations

We want to make it easy for people to test and learn, and remove barriers to doing it in situations where it works well. Through our accelerator projects and conversations with local partners and communities, we've found three main areas where strengthening the foundations would help:
So far, we have focused our efforts where we think we can have the biggest impact: tackling fragmented funding and showing how central and local government could work better together:

We're also exploring other areas where we can support the new model of government, including how the updated Magenta Book's new guidance on test and learn approaches can help embed this way of working more widely. Let us know what you think the biggest challenges are and what we could do about them!
What does it all mean?

We are putting people and communities at the centre of how public services are designed and delivered, making it easier to learn from what we do and improve continuously. Alongside this, we're building a community around test and learn, helping develop the skills and capabilities needed to sustain it and removing barriers to adopting this way of working.

There’s a lot to do in a short period of time but I’m optimistic about what's possible and proud of the progress we’re making. I feel lucky to work with brilliant people across government, local authorities, communities, delivery organisations and more who bring so much knowledge, passion and creativity to the table.

To follow along with our work, subscribe for email notifications using the sign-up link, or join our Test, Learn and Grow community on LinkedIn. Comment or reach out to us with any ideas, questions, feelings, thoughts; we want to hear from you!

title: Kinship care: turning ambition into lived experience

content.content: To mark the 10th anniversary of Kinship Care Week, National Kinship Care Ambassador, Dr Jahnine Davis, sets out why recognising kinship care is so important. From the National Kinship Standards to the Kinship Zones pilots, she explores what a genuine whole family approach looks like in practice, keeping children's voices central while supporting parents and carers throughout their kinship care journey.
A year of growing ambition

Over the past year, I have been encouraged by the growing ambition for kinship care across policy, practice, and reform. Kinship care is increasingly recognised not as a niche issue at the margins of children’s services, but as a vital part of our system of help, support, and protection.
That recognition matters, but recognition alone does not change children’s experiences. We need a deeper understanding of children’s lives and the relationships that shape them.

A whole family approach that keeps children at the centre must understand their identity, sense of belonging, and the relationships that matter most to them, and the support that helps them thrive. It must also recognise what parents, carers and wider family members need to sustain those relationships and provide children with stability.

The Government’s updated Kinship Care Statutory Guidance makes clear the role of kinship within the wider children’s social care reform landscape. It is critical to keeping more children safely within their family networks and supporting enduring relationships. Visibility of kinship care is also increasing with kinship carers included in Government’s review of parental leave, and kinship care being added as an indicator to the autumn school census. The Law Commission’s review of the legal framework underpinning kinship arrangements has the potential to address the challenges families have described for many years.
No single kinship experience

There is no single kinship experience. Special educational needs and/or disability, race and ethnicity, age, poverty, family circumstances, and community can all shape children’s and families’ experiences and the support they need.

That is why the new National Kinship Standards matter. I am proud to have led their development through engagement with children, kinship families and sector leaders. They provide a shared ambition for what positive support should look like and a basis for improving local practice.

Having national standards is not enough, their value will be determined by whether they strengthen leadership, improve accountability and create greater consistency in children’s and families’ experiences. Families experience support locally, where they live should not determine whether they are recognised, understood, or properly supported.
Learning from Kinship Zones

The Kinship Zones programme also gives us an opportunity to learn what a more joined-up approach can achieve. Across seven local authorities, it brings together a kinship allowance and Family Network Support Packages to explore how financial assistance, practical help and stronger family networks can support children to remain safely within their families.

Crucially, this is not only about what happens after a child moves into kinship care. Where children can remain safely with their parents, that support may prevent difficulties escalating. Where they cannot, the right support may enable a relative or family friend to offer a safe, stable, and loving home. Where a kinship arrangement is already in place, financial and wider support can help sustain it.
These are not separate ambitions. They are different points in the same journey.
A journey, not a destination

That same principle underpins the national research I am leading into children’s experiences of kinship care. This should be understood as a journey, not simply a destination. Listening to children throughout that journey, alongside understanding what their families need, will help shape policy, practice, and support.  Through visits and conversations with local authorities, I have seen determination, innovation, and a genuine willingness to understand what really makes a difference. Greater recognition does not automatically produce consistency, and policy ambition is not the same as lived experience.
What success will look like

The challenge now is to turn ambition into experiences that feel different for families. Do children feel seen, heard, and supported? Do carers receive help that reflects the realities they face? Are parents enabled to remain important in their lives where it is safe and appropriate? Can families access support throughout their journey rather than only when difficulties have become acute? Ultimately, are we helping children remain connected to the people who know them, love them, and are committed to them?
Kinship care is fundamentally about identity, belonging, and family connection.
There is much to be optimistic about, but there is still much to do. That challenge belongs to all of us.

title: Regulatory Policy Committee: Corporate Report 2025-26

content.content: The RPC has today published its corporate report for 2025-26, showcasing a year of strong performance, growing influence and continued commitment to improving the quality of evidence underpinning government regulation.

The report also highlights our wider work. This year, we have published guidance, engaged with stakeholders across business, academia and government, and strengthened international partnerships to promote evidence-based regulation.

A key theme of the year has been highlighting the importance of independent scrutiny - which has been strongly supported by business groups, Parliamentarians and other stakeholders. The RPC has continued to demonstrate the value that robust challenge brings to policymaking, helping ensure that regulatory decisions are informed by transparent, proportionate and credible evidence.

We would like to thank all those who have engaged with our work over the past year. We look forward to continuing our mission of supporting better regulation through independent scrutiny and evidence-based analysis.

title: RPC publishes new regulatory scorecard case histories guidance

content.content: We are pleased to announce the publication of the RPC's new regulatory scorecard case histories guidance. The document is designed to help policy teams across Whitehall develop stronger regulatory scorecards within options assessments (OAs) and impact assessments (IAs), improving the way they assess and communicate the impacts of regulatory proposals. The guidance draws on examples from published OAs and IAs and aims to support departments in producing proportionate, transparent and well-evidenced analysis.

The regulatory scorecard was introduced in 2023 as part of the reforms to the Better Regulation Framework. It provides a summary of the impacts of regulation on businesses, households and wider society, bringing together both monetised and non-monetised impacts alongside consideration of wider government priorities such as innovation, trade, investment, and natural capital and decarbonisation.
Key highlights of the new guidance
Assessing impacts proportionately

The guidance emphasises the importance of proportionate analysis. Departments are encouraged to tailor the level of evidence and quantification to the scale of the proposal while setting out plans for further analysis where policies are still at an early stage. It also highlights that expectations will increase as proposals move from OA stage to final-stage IA, with greater quantification and monetisation expected as evidence develops.
Presenting impacts clearly

The guidance provides practical advice on presenting impacts within the scorecard. It explains how departments should approach key metrics such as Net Present Social Value (NPSV), Equivalent Annual Net Direct Cost to Business (EANDCB) and Equivalent Annual Net Direct Cost to Households (EANDCH), while also ensuring that important non-monetised impacts are described where reliable quantification is not possible. The scorecard should act as a concise summary of the analysis, with detailed calculations and assumptions presented elsewhere in the OA or IA.
Considering wider government priorities

Part B of the scorecard requires departments to consider wider impacts, including effects on the business environment, international trade and investment, and natural capital and decarbonisation. The guidance encourages departments to draw on evidence and existing literature to explain how proposals may affect these areas and to ensure that assessments are specific to the policy being considered rather than generic statements.
Case studies and best practice

As with other RPC guidance, the document includes a range of case histories drawn from recently published OAs and IAs. These examples demonstrate good practice in presenting monetised and non-monetised impacts, assessing impacts on businesses and households, explaining distributional effects and considering wider government priorities. They also highlight common issues identified through RPC scrutiny and show how departments can address them.

The publication of this guidance reflects the RPC's continued commitment to improving the quality of regulatory appraisal across government. Recent scrutiny found that 22% of OAs and IAs received a 'weak' or 'very weak' rating for their assessment of impacts within the regulatory scorecard. The new guidance has therefore been produced to clarify expectations and support departments in developing more robust assessments.

We hope these case histories will provide a practical resource for policy teams and analysts as they develop future regulatory proposals. We welcome feedback on our work and encourage stakeholders to share their views on how we can continue to improve our guidance and processes.

title: A faster start to local plan-making: introducing the 'Submit a site for a local plan' tool

content.content: Before any new home is built, a suitable site has to be identified. Developers, landowners and members of the public can put forward sites through a call for sites process, carried out by every local planning authority (LPA). Planning officers then assess the sites against a number of measures and the successful ones are put forward as allocations for development in the area's local plan.

Right now the call for sites process is slow and inconsistent. Councils build their own web forms or wade through email submissions with reams of attachments, alongside static maps and spreadsheets. Every authority does it differently and that costs everyone time.
One planning officer told us:
During our research, we have heard versions of this story over and over again. This is the problem we want to solve and design out of the system.

We want local plans to be faster to produce, and to cover more of the country, so that decisions about housing and development can be made locally, and so communities get the homes and infrastructure they need sooner.

The new local plans system is now live, and we're continuing to test and learn where digital approaches can speed things up, helping LPAs prepare and adopt a local plan within 30 months. We've been exploring where the local plan process takes the most time, and where digital approaches could help. Site identification kept coming up as one of the earliest, most repeated steps in need of standardisation, which made it a natural place to focus our efforts. The lessons we learn here will also help us increase our understanding of how digital approaches could support other parts of the plan-making process.
The 'Submit a site for a local plan' is the latest tool, and we're keen to start testing it with LPAs on the real call for sites procedure for their next local plan.
What the tool is

The 'Submit a site for a local plan' tool will be a free, standardised online form that lets anyone – a landowner, developer, agent or member of the public – put forward a site, and submit it straight to their LPA in a consistent format. The tool will gather information on the site, its constraints and its potential for development. Submitters will be able to draw the site boundary directly on a map, with no GIS software needed. LPAs will be able to receive the information ready to use, with boundaries automatically converted into mapping data, and no manual re-entry required.

The tool builds on national guidance, published last year, on selecting, identifying and assessing sites for local plans. The guidance tells LPAs what to collect but it doesn't give them a consistent way to collect it. This tool seeks to standardise how site information is gathered. LPAs will still decide which sites are suitable and appropriate for their area using a variety of tools and processes to make assessments. What changes is how much time and effort they spend to get the site information in front of them in a usable form, so that they can make their assessments faster.

The tool doesn't replace the commercial digital tools some councils already use to help with their call for sites process, such as site assessment or viability analysis. It simply makes sure the site information being captured at the start is consistent. The ambition is that by capturing this information consistently at this point, it should make it easier for councils and the property technology industry to bring forward commercial tools to use and build on this baseline.
You can read more about how councils are already using digital tools for site identification and assessment in our guidance and case studies.
Help us test it

We have built this tool, based on research and interviews with people involved in all aspects of the site identification process. We're now looking for a small group of LPAs to help us test and embed it further.

If your LPA is planning to launch a call for sites round in the next 3-6 months, you could help shape a tool that aims to save your team and the people submitting sites to you, a significant amount of time, working and learning alongside our team at the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.
If you have any questions or are interested in getting involved, contact planmakingteam@communities.gov.uk.

title: Regulating a nuclear reactor through decommissioning

content.content: In 2022, after 46 years of generation, Hinkley Point B (HPB) switched off its last operational reactor and began defueling. The Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR) declared the site free of nuclear fuel in January 2026. Alister, our Hinkley Point B nuclear regulator, explains how the Environment Agency is regulating the power station as it moves to the next stage of the nuclear life cycle.
What’s happening at Hinkley Point B?

On 1 October 2026 Hinkley Point B’s environmental permits transferred from EDF to Nuclear Restoration Services (NRS), marking the start of the next step of the decommissioning journey. Decommissioning of Advanced Gas Cooled Reactor (AGR) sites is led by NRS, and HPB is the first AGR in England to transfer, following Hunterston B in Scotland in April.
Who regulated HPB before the Environment Agency?

Hinkley Point B began generating in 1976. During the station’s lifespan environmental law and protection has continued to evolve as our scientific knowledge and understanding has progressed. Before 1996 most environmental regulation of HPB was carried out by Her Majesty’s Inspectorate of Pollution (HMIP) and its predecessors. The big change to environmental regulation of nuclear power stations came in 1996 with the formation of the Environment Agency.
Environment Agency regulation - from the 1990s to 2025

We’ve been regulating Hinkley Point B for 30 years. Operators of nuclear sites must have an environmental permit for radioactive substances activities (RSR). The RSR permit for Hinkley Point B contains strict conditions (rules) that operators must always follow. We set limits on what they are allowed to release when carrying out certain activities such as disposing of radioactive waste or discharging to air and water into the environment.
Read more about our regulation during the operational phase on our previous blog.

In June 2025, EDF asked to change its radioactive substances permit. The reactors were no longer operational, and the site was fuel free. Environmental permits must represent the activities taking place and the changes reflected the reducing radiological hazard and risk from HPB. Similar changes can be seen at other sites as they move through decommissioning phases.

In July 2025 we received a joint application for the transfer of the radioactive substances permit from the current operator EDF to a new operator, NRS. It has been a huge team effort and, with our colleagues in Wessex area and our National Permitting Service, we’ve also transferred the Water Discharge Activity Permit, two closed landfill permits, a Combustion activity permit and a water abstraction activity. The permit for the District Survey Laboratory at Combwich was surrendered, with laboratory activities moving to the HPB site. As part of the surrender EDF demonstrated, through a final radiological survey, the absence of radioactive material and contamination within the laboratory facility.

Our regulation includes asking HPB to monitor its radioactive discharges and waste. We carry out our own independent monitoring to reassure both ourselves and the public and publish the results in our annual report.
What will regulation at HPB look like in the future?

We will continue to regulate HPB through decommissioning, ensuring the environment is protected and the management of radioactive waste is fully considered along with sustainability and the ability to mitigate and adapt to climate change.

We have many years of experience regulating decommissioning nuclear facilities. An example of this is next door at Hinkley Point A (HPA). HPA has seen many changes on site since it stopped generating in 2000, with the removal of plant, the installation of waste treatment and storage facilities and remediation of land.

During decommissioning activities include a focus on reduction of hazards (radiological, chemical). Since defueling HPB has been removing environmental hazards on site including bulk storage of oils and chemicals. This year our regulation has focused on EDF maintaining compliance with current permit conditions, processing the permit transfer and seeking assurances that the transition from EDF to NRS meets our requirements.

Going forward we’ll initially focus on how well the site has transitioned and adjusted to a new operator. Our role is to ensure that the operator has managed this change process and is still compliant with our permits. We’ll also learn lessons which we can apply to the permit transfer process for the remaining AGR fleet. NRS will also be developing and progressing decommissioning plans – and we’ll provide advice and guidance and ensure they comply with the requirements of the permit and BAT.

Community engagement will remain an important part of my role. We’ll continue to run our own ‘meet the regulator’ meetings, attend and report to the Site Stakeholder Group and respond to general enquiries from the community about our regulation of the site.
If you’ve got any questions about our work at Hinkley Point B contact us at nuclear@environment-agency.gov.uk

title: Helping young people turn experience into opportunity: introducing the Employability Skills Framework, by Gemma Marsh

content.content: Every young person develops valuable skills throughout their lives.

Whether it is balancing study with caring responsibilities, captaining a sports team, volunteering in their community, organising events, or completing coursework projects, young people gain capabilities that employers consistently tell us matter in the workplace.
Yet too often these skills go unrecognised.

When I speak to young people, they tell me that they struggle to explain how their experiences demonstrate skills that are relevant to work, while employers can find it difficult to identify potential in candidates who have limited employment history. To help bridge that gap, Skills England is today publishing the Employability Skills Framework.
The framework builds on Skills England’s Standard Skills Classification and other skills frameworks including Skills Builder and the Essential Digital Skills Framework.

It is available for everyone to use. We will continue to evolve it through further engagement to understand the needs to employers, young people, Strategic Authorities, providers and other stakeholders.
Creating a shared language for employability
We have identified 13 key employability skills:
For each skill, the Employability Skills Framework shows:
Using technology
The world of work is changing rapidly.

As digital technologies become increasingly important across sectors, young people need the confidence to use technology effectively while applying critical thinking and judgement. That is why digital literacy and AI-enabled capabilities are embedded throughout the framework. The focus is not simply on using technology, but on using it responsibly, evaluating outputs and maintaining human oversight.
This reflects what employers are increasingly telling us they need: individuals who can combine technical capability with communication, teamwork, adaptability and sound judgement.
How the framework supports young people
The skills listed above can be demonstrated through activities that young people are already doing.  For example:
The below helps to demonstrate how young people can turn this experience into evidence.
How the framework supports employers

The employers I speak to are passionate about creating opportunities for young people. Their advice is often that the best approach is not to ask young people to share their previous work experience, but instead to ask them about challenges they have overcome, times they’ve worked with others or organised things.
This helps young people to make that connection with the skills they have, which they may not yet be ready to express in the way we as employers are used to hearing.
Looking ahead

This publication represents an important step in Skills England's wider work to improve outcomes for young people and support employers to access the talent they need.  The framework has been developed with the support of the King's Trust, St Martin's Group, Youth Futures Foundation, and the North West Business Leaders Team.

Ultimately, our goal is simple: to help every young person recognise the value of the skills they already possess and to ensure employers can identify, recruit and develop potential wherever it is found.
Because opportunity should not depend on whether you have had a job before. It should depend on what you are capable of achieving.

title: Representation Matters: We Belong In Every Story. See Us. Hear Us. Read Us.

content.content: The National Year of Reading 2026 is the biggest campaign in a generation designed to help more people discover and rediscover the joy of reading and make it part of their everyday lives.
Public libraries have been at the heart of the campaign welcoming new visitors, hosting creative events, and celebrating the joy of reading in every community.
Today’s blog has been written by Hackney Libraries sharing their reflections on the National Year of Reading in the communities they serve.
Representation Matters: We Belong In Every Story. See Us. Hear Us. Read Us.

There is an undeniable energy that fills a library when a child sees themselves reflected in the pages of a book for the very first time. It is a moment of validation - a sudden realisation that their story, their background, and their voice truly matter. This was the electric spirit that defined the 2026 Children’s Black Book Fair UK at Dalston CLR James Library this August. With over 2,500 people joining us for this third annual celebration, it is clear that this fair is no longer just an event; it is a movement.

As we mark the National Year of Reading 2026, we’ve been reflecting on what it truly means to get a nation reading. At Hackney Libraries, we believe that reading for pleasure is the single biggest indicator of a child’s future success, but we also know that the playing field hasn’t always been level. If we are serious about the National Year of Reading, we must be serious about representation. We cannot simply tell children to read; we must provide the "mirrors" they need to see themselves reflected in the stories we offer.

That is exactly why this fair, delivered in deep partnership with LIT Stars CIC, has become such a flagship of our service. It’s an explicit recognition that libraries are essential social infrastructure, and they must be inclusive, vibrant hubs for every member of our community.

The day itself was a whirlwind of culture, creativity, and connection. From the moment the fair was officially opened by the legendary poet Linton Kwesi Johnson, the library was buzzing. We transformed Dalston Square into a vibrant Young Entrepreneur Market, giving young people aged under 25 a platform to showcase their talent. Inside, the library was alive with energy: families packed the storytelling marathons, children explored the "Eric Huntley Corner" to learn about our literary history, and the "Free Book Stop" - supported by our partners and the National Literacy Trust - ensured that children left with books they could own and cherish.

One of the most powerful moments for us was the unveiling of the "Hackney Writers Legacy Steps." This youth-led installation, which transformed our main staircase into a tribute to 48 Hackney-connected authors, poets, and storytellers, was a triumph. Conceived, designed, and delivered by our CBBF UK Youth Focus Group, these steps were a powerful reminder that our young people aren't just readers - they are creators, curators, and future legends in the making.

This fair is the "loudest" moment of our year, but it is supported by a year-round commitment. We work with LIT Stars CIC to ensure that Black literature is not a seasonal topic, but a central, consistent part of our collection and programming. The National Year of Reading has given us an incredible framework to highlight this work, but the daily reality for our staff - from the archives team to our library officers - is a constant, tireless mission to dismantle barriers to literacy.

Whether we are hosting reading or writing groups, homework or chess clubs, or curating diverse reading lists, we are aiming to reach the families who have historically felt sidelined by mainstream services. By making the library a sanctuary where African and African Caribbean culture is celebrated, we are not just helping children develop their reading skills; we are fostering a sense of belonging that lasts long after the fair has ended.

We are so proud of what the Children’s Black Book Fair UK achieved this year. It proved that when you combine grassroots passion with the institutional support of a local library, you create something transformative. As we continue through the National Year of Reading, we invite everyone to remember our theme: "We belong in every story." We are committed to making sure that every child in Hackney - and beyond - sees their own story reflected in the books we share.

We’re already looking forward to next year, but for now, we’re still riding the wave of an incredible August day. If you haven't been down to Dalston CLR James Library to see the Legacy Steps yet, we hope you will - they are on display throughout Black History Season and a reminder that in Hackney, great stories are written every single day.
About LIT Stars

LIT Stars CIC is a community-focused social enterprise dedicated to addressing the lack of representation of Black writers, characters, and stories in children’s literature. At Hackney Libraries, we know that without their partnership and invaluable contributions, we could never have achieved the incredible scale or impact of this project. Headed up by Juliet Coley, Romeo Bremmer, Yasmin McKenzie, and Cristina Cabral, the team brings a deep understanding of representation and the profound, transformative effect these stories have on our communities. They value the arts as an essential path to literacy and belonging, and their deep local knowledge and unique ability to connect with underserved families have been truly indispensable to our library service and mission.

title: Proud of What We Have Built Together

content.content: This month in our Blog - our Deputy Director Dr Victoria Hanna reflects on the progress Going Forward into Employment (GFiE) has made.
When I think about what Going Forward into Employment (GFiE) is doing, I feel an enormous sense of pride.

GFiE started in 2018 with a simple but important ambition: to create meaningful opportunities in the Civil Service for people facing barriers to employment. Since then, that ambition has grown into something much bigger…a network of colleagues, partners and champions across the UK who believe in the power of opportunity.   GFiE operates across regional hub locations throughout the UK, matching talent with vacancies to ensure high-calibre candidates find Civil Service opportunities right in the communities where they live.

Today, GFiE connects people from a wide range of backgrounds with real roles across the Civil Service, including people with convictions, veterans, carers, care-experienced people, autistic people and people from low socio-economic backgrounds. More than 4500 people have joined the Civil Service through GFiE since 2018, and there have been more than 1,000 appointments in the last two years alone.
But the numbers only tell part of the story.

What makes me proudest is the network behind those numbers. It is the colleagues who challenge traditional recruitment approaches. The recruiting and line managers who see potential rather than barriers.

The buddies who provide encouragement and support. Our partners in local government, the wider public sector and civil society who help us reach talented people we might otherwise never meet. And, of course, the candidates themselves, who bring their skills, resilience and lived experience into our organisation.
None of this has been achieved by one team. It has been achieved by an extended community of people willing to think differently, collaborate and open doors. Thank you.

GFiE has shown what is possible when we look beyond conventional routes into employment and recognise talent wherever it exists. What our network has achieved together is amazing  and it’s exciting to think about what we can achieve next.

Thank you everyone for your support, and for your vision. GFiE focuses on opening doors to talent, it changes lives and reaches into communities. Together we are making the Civil Service stronger through the people we bring into it.

title: Environmental permits: why they matter and how we're making it quicker to get one

content.content: Every year, the Environment Agency processes over 13,000 permit applications.

These decisions cover an enormous range of activity. From a small waste transfer site to permits regulating how the nation handles nuclear waste, every single one matters because they protect the air, land and water we all depend on.
This blog explains what an environmental permit is, why we're transforming how our permitting service works, and what this means for applicants.
What is an environmental permit for, and who needs one?

An environmental permit sets the conditions under which someone can carry out an activity that could affect the environment. That means if someone wants to operate with the potential to cause pollution, increase the risk of flooding, or affect land drainage or water resources, it needs our permission. Check if you need one here.

When applying, the business explains how they will meet the standards needed to protect the environment and human health under the Environmental Permitting Regulations (EPR). EPR protects air, land, water, people and nature by requiring measures that prevent environmental harm before it occurs.

We review whether the activity will meet EPR’s requirements and consult the public and professional partners where needed. If an application meets all legal and technical needs, and there are no grounds for refusal under the relevant legislation, we can issue the permit.
How the permitting system is changing

We oversee more than 100,000 permits across waste, water, industrial emissions, flood risk and radioactive substances. That variety brings real complexity, handled every day by our regulatory professionals. But it also highlights real opportunities to improve how the system works.
Businesses have told us they want more certainty about timescales, and communities have told us they want more transparency about how decisions are made.

That's why we're making targeted improvements across guidance, digital tools and processes to make permitting faster, clearer and more consistent, without ever compromising on the scrutiny that higher-risk permits need.
By March 2029, we've committed to determining 95% of permits on time. We're already there for our simplest permits, and we're building that same standard across every category.
What does this mean for people applying for permits?

We're already starting to see real results. Our backlog is down over three-quarters, queue times are at a three-year low, and we are now processing 83% of all permitting applications on time. Enhanced validation has also cut determination times for complex applications by roughly 100 days.

This progress is being delivered through a broader set of changes, including new digital services, clearer guidance, and dedicated support for the most complex projects. Here's what that looks like in practice.

The Apply for and Manage Environmental Permissions service will let businesses submit and manage environmental permissions online, end to end, for the first time. It's now publicly available for the application stage, covering activities from vehicle dismantling and metal recycling to waste storage and treatment, mobile plant deployments and herbicide agreements - with more services to follow.

The new Priority Tracked provides dedicated, wrap-around support for developments with multiple complex permitting needs over long durations. It's already supporting over 60 major developments across housing, energy, mining and technology.

Building on this progress, we've established Nature Permitting and Coordination, offering a single point of contact and coordinated support for nature recovery projects requiring multiple environmental permits and licences.
Together, these services are driving a more coordinated permitting service with better outcomes for sustainable growth and nature recovery.
What happens next, and how applicants can help speed things up

Businesses and investors need confidence that decisions will be timely and consistent. We continue to review the tools and guidance available to support a good-quality application. Equally, communities deserve confidence that those decisions will protect and enhance the environment they care about. We're working to deliver both.

You can help too. If you're applying for a permit, especially a complex one, you can use our pre-application service and provide complete, high-quality information from the start. Getting it right first time is the biggest thing you can do to help us decide faster.
Efficient and effective permitting is one of the strongest tools we have to protect homes and habitats while enabling the development the country needs, and we're making real progress.
For further updates, follow the Chief Regulator's LinkedIn page.

title: Evaluation of the TRA investigation process: insight from our stakeholders and staff
authors: Ilona Serwicka, Head of Evaluation and Research

content.content: Today we have published a research report prepared by an independent research agency, Savanta, for the Trade Remedies Authority (TRA). This report presents the findings of the agency’s evaluation of our investigation process, based on insights from external stakeholders and staff. The report also sets out improvement priorities and recommendations for the TRA.
The value of feedback in improving the TRA investigation process

Earlier this year, the agency approached both UK and non-UK organisations to invite them to complete a survey and participate in one-to-one interviews to describe their experiences of taking part in the TRA’s trade remedy investigations. The objective was to help us understand what works well in our investigation process and what could be improved, specifically:
Surveying stakeholders and staff – how the project was carried out

As part of its research, the agency contacted UK producers, UK importers, trade associations and business groups, legal advisers and legal representatives, as well as overseas exporters and overseas producers.

Organisations were firstly invited to complete a survey on their experience of engaging with the TRA and participating in the TRA’s trade remedy investigations. They were asked about their level of familiarity with the TRA and the TRA investigations, their satisfaction from engagement with the TRA, and investigation barriers and challenges.

Organisation were also invited to join follow-up one-to-one interviews with the agency to share more in-depth feedback. These semi-structured interviews, which ranged from 45 to 60 minutes and were conducted virtually, explored in detail motivation to participate in TRA investigations, barriers, challenges, pain points and recommended improvements.

The agency also surveyed TRA staff involved in case teams. This was done to compare internal and external perspectives on the strengths and shortcomings of the TRA investigation process. It also helped to gather insights into how well TRA staff understand stakeholders' experiences of TRA investigations, and the barriers and challenges they face.
What did the research conclude about the TRA investigation process: improvement priorities and recommendations

The organisations which participated in the research tended to have a good level of familiarity with the TRA: a third of respondents first engaged with the TRA five or more years ago, while another third first engaged three or four years ago.

Stakeholders praised TRA staff for their professionalism, responsiveness and procedural fairness. In particular, stakeholders valued the quality of direct communication with case teams, describing it as clear, supportive and constructive, as well as early and in-person contact, which was particularly valued by first-time participants.
Based on stakeholder and TRA staff responses, the report sets out five recommendations for the TRA.
Independent recommendations of the TRA investigation process evaluation research:

These reflect the experiences of current and previous case participants. As the TRA’s investigation process has developed since it was established in 2021, it’s helpful to set out areas where improvements have already been made or are in train, along with the further steps we intend to take in response to the report’s recommendations.
Improving the TRA investigation process for participants

In July 2025, we launched the Trade Remedies Advisory Service to provide improved support for businesses navigating trade remedy investigations. This built on the work of the TRA’s Pre-Application Office and now provides hands-on assistance to businesses looking to navigate trade remedies, both in making an application or engaging with investigations.

The new offer includes more proactive engagement with industries, including clear guidance through webinars for all interested parties, outreach targeting diverse industry sectors, demystifying application procedures, and dedicated SME industry support, as well as enhanced data monitoring to identify emerging trade concerns and industries requiring additional support.

In June 2026, we also launched a new version of the Trade Remedies Service (TRS) platform, through which stakeholders participate in and submit evidence for investigations. The new platform has been designed to improve usability, make processes clearer and enhance overall system functionality. It has been developed using feedback from users and informed by research and testing.

We understand the importance of transparent investigation timelines to provide greater certainty around case status, case progress and deadlines for case participants. We publish an external case timeline at the point of initiating an investigation, updating it if key dates change during an investigation. The external case timeline sets out dates of key milestones, including publication of questionnaires, questionnaire completion deadlines, verification and dates for our provisional and final determinations.
A final thought
This blog provides an overview of the research report and its main findings. For more detail, please see the research report.
If you did not take part in the independent research but would like to share your reflections on our investigation process, please contact us at: contact@traderemedies.gov.uk.
